A plain map's default method and a concurrent map's override can have different atomicity guarantees, so I do not infer cross-thread safety from the method name alone. I define duplicate policy before accumulating records.

followups.q: What happens if the remapping function returns null?
followups.a: The mapping is removed.

followups.q: Does merge automatically make a HashMap concurrent-safe?
followups.a: No. The map implementation determines concurrency guarantees.

questions.trap: Using merge with an order-dependent or side-effecting reducer and assuming stable results.
questions.notes: Unverified estimate; frequency is an unverified estimate; merge atomicity depends on the map implementation.

questions.question: What do Collections.checkedList and related wrappers protect against?
questions.answer: A checked collection wrapper validates elements passed through that wrapper against a runtime Class token, catching some heap-pollution mistakes at insertion time. It is especially useful when a legacy raw-type API could otherwise insert an incompatible object into a generically typed collection. It does not validate every existing element retroactively, does not deep-check nested generic arguments and can be bypassed by another reference to the original collection. The wrapper is also not a substitute for compile-time generics. I use it at boundaries where raw interoperability is unavoidable and make sure all mutation paths use the checked view.

followups.q: Does a checked wrapper validate List<List<String>> recursively?
followups.a: No; the runtime class token cannot verify erased nested generic arguments.

followups.q: Can another alias bypass the wrapper?
followups.a: Yes; direct mutation of the backing collection avoids wrapper checks.

questions.trap: Treating a checked wrapper as deep validation or assuming it controls every alias to the backing collection.
questions.notes: Unverified estimate; runtime checks are limited by type erasure.

questions.question: What constraints apply to Collections.newSetFromMap?
questions.answer: Collections.newSetFromMap creates a Set backed by a supplied Map, letting a suitable map determine membership semantics and ordering. The map must be empty when passed, and the set becomes its controlling view; callers should not keep mutating the map independently. The map's key equality, iteration and concurrency behavior shape the resulting set. An IdentityHashMap can therefore create an identity-based set for specialized object graphs, while a LinkedHashMap can preserve insertion order. I use this factory only when a map-backed set behavior is actually needed, otherwise a standard Set implementation is clearer.

followups.q: Can the supplied map already contain mappings?
followups.a: No; the API requires it to be empty when creating the set.

followups.q: What controls uniqueness in the resulting set?
followups.a: The backing map's key semantics, including its equality or identity behavior.

questions.trap: Continuing to mutate the backing map independently after handing it to the set view.
questions.notes: Unverified estimate; API preconditions should be checked against Java 21 documentation.

questions.question: What workload suits CopyOnWriteArraySet, and why can writes be costly?
questions.answer: CopyOnWriteArraySet is a set backed by copy-on-write array behavior, useful when iteration greatly outnumbers updates and the set remains relatively small. Iterators observe a snapshot and do not support removal, while each successful modification can require copying the underlying array and checking for duplicates. This creates predictable traversal at the cost of write amplification and memory churn. It protects the collection structure, not mutable element objects. I consider it for small listener registries or rarely changed configuration, and use a different concurrent set when membership updates are frequent or cardinality is large.

followups.q: Will an existing iterator see a later set insertion?
followups.a: No; it traverses the snapshot captured when created.

followups.q: Is it suitable for a high-churn large set?
followups.a: Usually not, because writes copy array state and membership checks can be costly.

questions.trap: Choosing copy-on-write based only on safe iteration while ignoring update frequency and collection size.
questions.notes: Unverified estimate; collection selection estimate, not a core concurrency exercise.

questions.question: How do Set.of and Set.copyOf differ when the source contains duplicates?
questions.answer: Set.of takes explicit elements and rejects duplicate arguments, making accidental repeated constants visible. Set.copyOf accepts a collection and produces an unmodifiable set, with duplicate source elements represented once according to set semantics. Both reject null elements. Neither promises a particular iteration order, and neither deeply copies mutable element objects. I choose Set.of for a literal whose entries should be unique by construction and Set.copyOf for converting dynamic input after deciding whether deduplication is acceptable. If duplicates indicate invalid data rather than redundancy, validate before copying instead of silently collapsing them.

followups.q: What does Set.of do with duplicate arguments?
followups.a: It throws IllegalArgumentException.

followups.q: Does Set.copyOf preserve duplicate input elements?
followups.a: No; the result is a set and contains each equality-distinct element once.

questions.trap: Using Set.copyOf to hide duplicate input when duplicates should be reported as a data error.
questions.notes: Unverified estimate; Java 9/10+ factory APIs, Java 21 baseline.

questions.question: Can TreeMap accept null keys?
questions.answer: With natural ordering, TreeMap does not accept a null key because it cannot compare null to ordinary keys. A custom comparator may define an ordering that handles null, depending on the comparator and map operation, but relying on that should be explicit. Null values are a separate question and are permitted by TreeMap's general map contract, which can make get returning null ambiguous for absence. I usually reject null keys at the domain boundary and choose a clear comparator policy if null has real meaning. Sorting and uniqueness still depend on comparator consistency.

followups.q: Does natural-order TreeMap accept a null key?
followups.a: No; natural comparison cannot order a null key against normal keys.

followups.q: Can a custom comparator permit null?
followups.a: It can define null ordering, but that contract must be deliberate and consistently applied.

questions.trap: Assuming every sorted map has the same null-key behavior regardless of comparator.
questions.notes: Unverified estimate; null behavior should be checked against the configured comparator and operations.

questions.question: When are ConcurrentHashMap.size and mappingCount unsuitable as control-flow gates?
questions.answer: ConcurrentHashMap.size returns an int, while mappingCount returns a long for larger counts. During concurrent updates, aggregate status methods can describe a transient state rather than one atomic snapshot; they are useful for monitoring or estimates but should not decide a correctness-critical action such as whether capacity is available. A check followed by a separate update can race even if the reported count was accurate at the instant observed. I encode capacity or admission policy in an atomic operation or explicit coordination instead of treating size as a reservation. This is a collection contract distinction, not a transaction across external systems.

followups.q: Why does mappingCount return long?
followups.a: It can represent a mapping count larger than the int range of size().

followups.q: Can size followed by put enforce a hard capacity?
followups.a: No. Another update can occur between observation and insertion.

questions.trap: Using a concurrent map's current size as an atomic capacity reservation.
questions.notes: Unverified estimate; directly supports supplied ConcurrentHashMap internals GAP; status methods are intended for estimates under concurrent updates.

questions.question: Which data structure backs ArrayList, and how does it differ from the List interface?
questions.answer: List is an interface that defines the contract; ArrayList is one implementation. Internally ArrayList stores elements in an Object[] that is allocated lazily, with a default capacity of 10 on the first add. When the array is full it grows by about 1.5 times, the old capacity plus half, and copies the elements. get by index is O(1), appending is amortised O(1), and inserting or removing in the middle is O(n) because later elements shift. Declare variables as List<T> and choose the implementation at construction. LinkedList trades fast end operations for O(n) indexed access.

followups.q: What does ensureCapacity help with?
followups.a: Pre-sizing before a known bulk insert so the array is not copied repeatedly.

followups.q: When would you pick LinkedList instead?
followups.a: Rarely. ArrayDeque or ArrayList usually win in practice, so justify LinkedList with a measured need.

questions.trap: Saying ArrayList doubles its capacity, or that LinkedList is faster for inserts without counting the O(n) cost of reaching the position.
questions.notes: Reported in user-provided interview notes, item 2.1 (company not recorded). Model answer written for this handbook, not copied from the notes. Related: JH-S02-029, JH-S02-053.

questions.question: What is HashMap's time complexity for get and put, and how does heavy collision change it?
questions.answer: With a good hash function, get, put and remove are O(1) on average. If many keys land in one bucket, Java 7 scanned a linked list, so the worst case was O(n). Since Java 8 a bin with at least 8 entries is converted to a red-black tree once the table has at least 64 buckets, giving O(log n) lookups when keys are Comparable or otherwise orderable; below 6 entries it reverts to a list on resize. Tree lookups for keys that are neither Comparable nor well hashed can still degrade, so a good hashCode remains the real defence. containsValue is O(n) and iteration costs O(capacity + size).

followups.q: Why does treeification need a table capacity of at least 64?
followups.a: With a small table the JDK prefers to resize, which spreads keys across more buckets, rather than build trees.

followups.q: Why is a poor hashCode dangerous in production?
followups.a: Many keys in one bucket turn lookups into list or tree scans, and attackers can exploit this as hash flooding.

questions.trap: Quoting O(1) without qualification, or claiming Java 8 makes the worst case O(1).
questions.notes: Reported in user-provided interview notes, item 2.3 (Morgan Stanley (Synechron)). Model answer written for this handbook, not copied from the notes. Related: JH-S02-001, JH-S02-022, JH-S02-030.

questions.question: A class overrides hashCode to return 1 and equals to return true. Two instances are put into a HashMap with different values. What are the size and the results of get?
questions.answer: The size is 1. Both keys hash to the same bucket, and when the second put walks that bucket it calls equals against the first key, which returns true, so HashMap treats it as the same key and only replaces the value. The stored key remains the first object, and get with either instance returns the second value. This shows why hashCode and equals must agree: equal objects must have equal hash codes. If only hashCode were overridden, equals would use identity and the size would be 2, a chain in one bucket. If only equals were overridden, the two objects usually hash to different buckets, so lookups can fail even for equal keys.

followups.q: What changes if hashCode returns 1 but equals is not overridden?
followups.a: equals falls back to identity, so both entries are kept in one bucket as a chain and the size is 2.

followups.q: What changes if only equals is overridden?
followups.a: Identity hash codes usually differ, so the keys land in different buckets and get() may not find an equal key.

questions.trap: Answering size 2 by assuming a different object means a different key. HashMap decides with the hash and equals only.
questions.notes: Reported in user-provided interview notes, item 2.4 (Accolite). Model answer written for this handbook, not copied from the notes. Related: JH-S01-001, JH-S02-005.

questions.question: Which concurrent queue implementations does java.util.concurrent offer, and when do you pick each?
questions.answer: ConcurrentLinkedQueue is unbounded and non-blocking, built on compare-and-swap, for high-throughput hand-offs where nothing needs to wait. LinkedBlockingQueue supports blocking put and take with an optional bound and is the classic producer-consumer queue behind fixed thread pools. ArrayBlockingQueue is a bounded array queue with optional fairness, useful for back-pressure. PriorityBlockingQueue orders elements by a comparator and is unbounded. DelayQueue releases elements only after their delay expires, which suits scheduling and retries. SynchronousQueue has no capacity and hands each item directly to a waiting consumer, which cached thread pools use.

followups.q: Why is an unbounded queue risky behind a thread pool?
followups.a: If producers outpace consumers it grows until memory is exhausted; prefer a bounded queue with a rejection policy.

followups.q: Which queue gives back-pressure naturally?
followups.a: A bounded blocking queue, since put blocks, or offer fails, when it is full.

questions.trap: Treating all queues as interchangeable and ignoring boundedness and blocking behaviour.
questions.notes: Reported in user-provided interview notes, item 2.6 (Accolite). Model answer written for this handbook, not copied from the notes. Related: JH-S05-008, JH-S05-014.
